claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by a mechanically robust, self-healing passive film at grain boundaries.
Chemical heterogeneity inherent in high-entropy alloys enables formation of the proposed grain-boundary passive film.
The initial high-entropy alloy has a homogeneous multi-principal-element composition.
Passive-film-forming elements such as Cr and Al are concentrated at grain boundaries and secondary phases in the proposed alloy.
Grain boundaries enriched in film-forming elements support rapid formation and regeneration of a protective passive film.
Finely dispersed secondary phases support rapid formation and regeneration of a protective passive film.
Chemical heterogeneity facilitates development of a continuous passive film at grain boundaries.
The grain-boundary passive film is self-healing.
The passive film mitigates corrosive attack.
The passive film resists mechanical removal during wear.
Rapid passive-film reformation counteracts wear-induced loss of protection under combined wear and corrosion.
An alloy with optimal film-forming chemistry will have a lower wear rate under combined degradation than a matched alloy with suppressed passive-film formation.
An alloy with optimal film-forming chemistry will have shallower corrosion penetration under combined degradation than a matched alloy with suppressed passive-film formation.
Combined degradation in the film-promoting alloy will be less severe than the sum expected from independent wear and corrosion effects.
Reducing the concentration or connectivity of film-forming elements at grain boundaries diminishes self-healing passive-film capability.
The protective effect should persist under continuous moderate-to-severe combined wear and corrosive exposure.
The protective benefit may disappear when mechanical removal irreversibly disrupts the passive film faster than it reforms.
The protective benefit may disappear when corrosion aggressiveness exceeds the passive film's chemical robustness.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as compositionally homogeneous, while the hypothesis and mediator require inherent chemical heterogeneity, grain-boundary enrichment, and secondary-phase partitioning. This could be reconciled by distinguishing nominal bulk homogeneity from nanoscale or interfacial segregation, but that distinction is not stated.
